title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction
authors: Aamod Varma, Shuyi Jia, Victor Fung
abstract: Diffusion-based pretraining has emerged as a powerful strategy for learning transferable representations in graph neural networks for materials property prediction without requiring quantum-mechanical labels such as energies, forces, and stresses for every pretraining structure. However, the method retains a critical dependency: it requires structures residing near local minima of a potential energy surface, which have traditionally been obtained through costly DFT relaxations of known or physically synthesized compounds. This reliance constrains both the scale and the structural diversity of available pretraining data, leaving large regions of crystal structure space unexplored. In this work, we connect diffusion-based pretraining with synthetic structure generation to reduce this bottleneck. We introduce a synthetic data generation pipeline combining three complementary strategies: perturb-and-relax, generative sampling via MatterGen, and protostructure enumeration. Where structural relaxation is required, we use fast machine-learned interatomic potentials instead of performing a new DFT relaxation for each generated structure. We further compare a coordinate-denoising control with continuous-time variance-preserving (VP) and sub-VP diffusion objectives using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone. The source comparison covers seven MatBench property-prediction tasks, and an eighth task, \texttt{mp\_gap}, is included in the protostructure scaling study. Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically outperforms random initialization on all seven source-comparison tasks. Scaling the protostructure corpus from 20k to 165k under a fixed 400-epoch schedule numerically matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks; because this protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, the result reflects joint data-and-compute scaling.

infographic.key_insight: Synthetic crystal structures can support diffusion pretraining for materials property prediction while reducing dependence on costly DFT-relaxed structures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast machine-learned interatomic potentials enable larger, more structurally diverse pretraining datasets without requiring a new DFT relaxation for every generated crystal.
method: Generate structures through perturb-and-relax, MatterGen sampling, and protostructure enumeration.
Use machine-learned interatomic potentials where structural relaxation is required.
Compare coordinate denoising with continuous-time VP and sub-VP diffusion using a randomly initialized Orb-v2 backbone.
infographic.evidence_signal: Every synthetic-pretraining condition numerically beats random initialization across seven MatBench tasks; scaling protostructures from 20k to 165k matches or exceeds MP-20k pretraining on most tasks in an eight-task scaling study.
infographic.watch_item: The fixed 400-epoch scaling protocol increases both data diversity and optimization updates, so gains cannot be attributed to dataset size alone.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Crystal Data Generation for Diffusion Pretraining in Material Property Prediction

title: Weight-Space Programming for Materials Science
authors: Sk Md Ahnaf Akif Alvi, Raymundo Arróyave
abstract: A materials discovery campaign often begins with almost no measurements of the property it is searching for, and the models that rank candidates or screen the output of a generator then have to be built from those first few labels. Following recent work on weight-space programming, in which a language model writes the weights of a small network directly as text, we show that a general-purpose model, given the task in words, the names of the inputs and a network of 16 hidden units with every weight set to zero, can provide this starting point by filling in all of the weights from what it has learned about materials. With no labels, the networks of the strongest model rank experimental alloys at Spearman co-efficient = 0.64 to 0.79, where the best of five simple descriptors reaches 0.47 to 0.62. They rank the bulk modulus of crystals added during generative discovery loops at 0.95, where the inverse volume per atom reaches 0.89, and 35 phase-equilibrium targets computed with Thermo-Calc at a mean of 0.67, close to the 0.70 of an extrapolation from calculated binary and ternary data. As the prior mean of a Gaussian process they raise the ranking at five labels from 0.35 to 0.69 on alloys and from 0.15 to 0.95 on crystals, and they lower the regret of Bayesian optimization significantly on 4 of 5 experimental tasks and on 13 to 16 of 33 computed targets, depending on how multiple tests are corrected, without raising it significantly on any. The same networks also serve as the mean of a Bayesian neural network and as a screen for the samples of two crystal generators, where they do as well as standard models trained on 400 labeled structures. The gain is confined to the first tens of labels and to targets that no rule or sub-system extrapolation already ranks.

infographic.key_insight: A general-purpose language model can directly write a small neural network’s weights to rank materials without property labels and improve early-stage discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These label-free networks can initialize surrogate models and screen generated crystals when measurements are scarce.
method: Provide the language model with a task description, input names, and a zero-initialized network with 16 hidden units.
Have it fill in every network weight directly as text.
Use the network for ranking, as a Bayesian surrogate’s prior mean, or to screen generated candidates.
infographic.evidence_signal: At five labels, Gaussian-process ranking improved from Spearman 0.35 to 0.69 on alloys and 0.15 to 0.95 on crystals; Bayesian optimization regret fell significantly on 4 of 5 experimental tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits are confined to the first tens of labels and targets not already well ranked by simple rules or subsystem extrapolation.
infographic.paper_title: Weight-Space Programming for Materials Science

title: A Practitioner's Guide to Materials Theory and Computation in the Age of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence
authors: Jack Yang
abstract: Computational modelling has become a cornerstone of materials science, with advances in atomistic simulations, high-throughput computation, and artificial intelligence transforming how materials are understood, discovered, and designed. These developments build upon generations of theoretical innovations that have translated complex mathematical and physical principles into practical predictive tools. However, the growing diversity of computational methods presents challenges for practitioners seeking a coherent understanding of their theoretical foundations. Drawing upon the author's research experience, this monograph provides a practitioner-oriented, pedagogical overview of computational materials science, unified through the concepts of potential-energy landscapes and statistical sampling. It explores how these concepts underpin structural stability, phase behaviour, and electronic and magnetic properties, through a systematic treatment of empirical force fields, density-functional theory, many-body electronic-structure methods, statistical sampling, and property prediction. It further examines high-throughput workflows, materials databases, and the probabilistic foundations of artificial intelligence. Particular emphasis is placed on atomistic representations, graph neural networks, and generative models, highlighting the roles of symmetry, group theory, differential geometry, and stochastic processes in modern materials modelling. By connecting established physical theories with emerging data-driven approaches, this monograph offers a unified perspective on computational materials science and identifies opportunities and challenges toward physics-informed, efficient, and reliable materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: Potential-energy landscapes and statistical sampling provide a unified framework linking established materials theory with modern AI-driven discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This practitioner-oriented guide helps engineers connect atomistic simulations, property prediction, and data-driven workflows for materials discovery and design.
method: Connect force fields, density-functional theory, and many-body methods through shared physical concepts.
Explain statistical sampling, property prediction, high-throughput workflows, and materials databases.
Examine atomistic representations, graph neural networks, and generative models through symmetry and probabilistic foundations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a pedagogical monograph informed by the author's research experience, without reporting datasets, quantitative benchmarks, or comparative evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish the accuracy, efficiency, or reliability of any specific AI-driven discovery workflow.
infographic.paper_title: A Practitioner's Guide to Materials Theory and Computation in the Age of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence

title: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation
authors: Changzhi Ai, Xueping Qin, Dimosthenis Sokaras, Frank Abild-Pedersen, Johannes Voss
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) now approach density functional theory (DFT) accuracy at a fraction of its cost, but the practical benefit is limited by software fragmentation: each state-of-the-art architecture is released as a separate codebase, with its own data format, configuration system, training loop and molecular-dynamics interface. Comparing two architectures on the same dataset, or moving a trained model into a production simulation, therefore requires substantial re-engineering. We introduce IANN (InterAtomic Neural Network), an open-source PyTorch framework that reimplements equivariant graph neural networks - PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA - behind a unified data object, a unified trainer and a single deployment route, so that the architecture is a one-word change in a configuration dictionary. Forces, stresses and virials are obtained for every architecture from one analytic differentiation of the energy with respect to the edge vectors of the atomic graph, exact under periodic boundary conditions. Distributed training is configured automatically from the SLURM, PBS or MPI environment, so the same script runs unchanged from a workstation to a multi-node GPU allocation. Self-describing checkpoints serve directly as ASE calculators, as ensembles reporting uncertainties, or as TorchScript models run inside LAMMPS through bundled C++ pair styles with single- and multi-GPU inference. Trained on a common dataset of millions of structures, the architectures can be compared under identical conditions. We further release PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures from MPtrj, Alexandria, OMat24, MatPES, OC20, OC22, OC25, MPr2SCAN and MatPESr2SCAN, spanning the PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN functionals. Additionally, IANN provides an agent interface to facilitate integration with autonomous agents.

infographic.key_insight: IANN unifies seven equivariant interatomic neural network architectures in one PyTorch framework, making architecture selection a one-word configuration change.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A shared training and deployment workflow reduces re-engineering when comparing interatomic potentials or moving them into ASE and LAMMPS simulations.
method: Standardize atomic data, training and deployment across PaiNN, NequIP, MACE, Allegro, EquiformerV2, EquiformerV3 and UMA.
Derive forces, stresses and virials through analytic energy differentiation with respect to graph edge vectors, including periodic boundaries.
Automatically configure distributed training and deploy self-describing checkpoints through ASE or TorchScript-enabled LAMMPS interfaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports architecture comparisons on a common dataset of millions of structures and released PaiNN foundation models trained on 41.9 million curated DFT structures spanning PBE, RPBE and r2SCAN.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical accuracy or speed benchmarks, so performance and deployment efficiency require validation for the target simulation.
infographic.paper_title: IANN: A Unified Framework for Equivariant InterAtomic Neural Networks with User-Friendly Implementation

title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases
authors: Jiang Xiaobo, Dinghong Lai
abstract: Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) is an important step in accelerating the generation and discovery of new materials. In recent years, diffusion-based CSP methods have made significant progress. However, existing models still suffer from generation bias when facing diverse materials spaces, while systematic approaches for tracing the sources of such performance variations remain limited. To address this issue, we propose LAS (Layered Analysis Strategy), a mechanism analysis framework that identifies crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance as two key factors affecting generation difficulty and further reveals their relationships with model generation performance. Building on these findings, we further propose DSADiff (Data Structure-Aware Diffusion), a data structure-aware diffusion model that transforms the key factors identified by LAS into a unified generation difficulty representation and uses it to jointly drive feature modeling and training strategy optimization. This enables the model to adapt its representation and generation capability to samples with different data structures and difficulty levels, thereby mitigating learning bias across samples. Experiments on three CSP benchmark datasets, including Carbon-24, demonstrate that DSADiff consistently improves both Match Rate and RMSE, with a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods and achieving new state-of-the-art performance. This work deepens the understanding of diffusion-based CSP models from the perspective of generation bias and provides a new direction for designing less biased generative models for complex materials spaces.

infographic.key_insight: DSADiff targets generation biases linked to crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance to improve diffusion-based crystal structure prediction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More reliable structure prediction across diverse materials could support computational screening and materials discovery.
method: Use a Layered Analysis Strategy (LAS) to identify factors associated with generation difficulty.
Combine crystal complexity and elemental composition imbalance into a unified difficulty representation.
Use this representation to guide feature modeling and training strategy optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three CSP benchmarks, including Carbon-24, the abstract reports improved Match Rate and RMSE, a maximum Match Rate improvement of 9%, and state-of-the-art performance.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify computational overhead or whether the reported 9% Match Rate gain is relative or absolute.
infographic.paper_title: DSADiff: Data Structure-Aware Diffusion for Crystal Structure Prediction via Mitigating Complexity- and Imbalance-Induced Biases

title: Adsorbate-Free Screening of Dissociative Water Adsorption on Nickel Nanoparticles via Graph Neural Networks
authors: Marta Monti, Alec Noppe, Olivier Lugier, Maria B. Brands, Bernd Ensing
abstract: Dissociative water adsorption is a key step in heterogeneous and electrochemical catalysis, but on finite Ni nanosystems the OH$^*$ and H$^*$ fragments can occupy many combinations of surface sites, making exhaustive density functional theory (DFT) screening impractical. We introduce a graph neural network (GNN) framework with an adsorbate-free representation: candidate O- and H-binding sites are defined by sets of Ni atoms (\textit{anchors}), and each site pair is encoded as a graph constructed solely from these anchors and their local Ni environment. Using only MACE-relaxed bare Ni geometries as input, separate GNNs predict the DFT-reference adsorption energies of OH$^*$+H$^*$ configurations and whether the proposed binding sites would be retained upon DFT relaxation, eliminating the need to construct or relax adsorbates during screening. Trained across Ni nanoclusters and Ni(111)/Ni(100) surfaces, the energy model achieves a mean absolute error of 0.031 eV on the internal validation set and demonstrates transferability to unseen Ni$_{55}$, Ni$_{91}$, and Ni$_{130}$ clusters and larger surface cells, particularly for relative-energy ranking, although quantitative accuracy varies across systems. These independent tests also support the retention classifier's use as a conservative filter for selecting configurations likely to preserve their proposed binding sites. Application to Ni nanoparticles containing up to $\sim$3000 atoms identifies favorable co-adsorption motifs and shows that lower O-site coordination generally stabilizes the dissociated state, whereas H-site coordination has a weaker influence. The framework thus offers an efficient route to screening adsorption energetics, with potential extensions to other metals and adsorbate combinations.

infographic.key_insight: Graph neural networks predict dissociative water adsorption on nickel using only bare-metal geometry, avoiding adsorbate construction and relaxation during screening.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables efficient screening of OH*+H* binding configurations on nickel nanoparticles containing up to approximately 3,000 atoms.
method: Define candidate O- and H-binding sites using sets of nickel anchor atoms.
Build adsorbate-free graphs from anchors and their local environment in MACE-relaxed bare nickel structures.
Use separate GNNs to predict DFT-reference adsorption energies and binding-site retention after relaxation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The energy model achieved 0.031 eV internal-validation MAE, with independent tests on unseen Ni55, Ni91, and Ni130 clusters and larger surface cells supporting transferability, particularly for relative-energy ranking.
infographic.watch_item: Quantitative accuracy varies across systems, so predictions on new nanoparticle geometries require validation.
infographic.paper_title: Adsorbate-Free Screening of Dissociative Water Adsorption on Nickel Nanoparticles via Graph Neural Networks

title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms
authors: Austin H. Cheng, Marcel Müller, Andreas Burger, Yeonghun Kang, Tsz Wai Ko, Marta Skreta
abstract: Generative models play a rapidly growing role in the design and simulation of molecules. The most widely used applications of generative models are in large language models (LLMs), owing to the natural flexibility of language for specifying and answering queries. However, generalist LLMs do not effectively handle large sets of 3D coordinates, whereas specialist generative models of 3D molecules cannot reach the controllability afforded by language. To bridge these capabilities, we propose Nahual, a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion model for any sequence of text and 3D molecules. To enable expressive autoregression on continuous coordinates, we propose next-token diffusion, whereby a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to the clean tokens before it, without increasing context size. We train Nahual on a curated set of twelve 3D chemistry tasks ranging from microsolvation to molecular conformer search to adsorption on metal surfaces, with associated evaluation metrics and baselines. The result is a single set of end-to-end-trained weights that simultaneously performs all tasks and surpasses state-of-the-art models specialized for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation. Our results demonstrate the viability of scaling generalist decoder-only models for native multimodal understanding and generation across language and chemistry. Code is available at https://github.com/the-matter-lab/nahual.

infographic.key_insight: Nahual unifies language and 3D molecular generation in one decoder-only model, combining text-based control with native coordinate generation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A single model could support workflows spanning molecular conformer search, microsolvation, crystal structure prediction, and adsorption on metal surfaces.
method: Uses a decoder-only autoregressive diffusion architecture for sequences mixing text and 3D molecules.
Introduces next-token diffusion: a causal transformer denoises each token while attending to preceding clean tokens, without expanding context size.
Trains one shared set of weights end to end across twelve 3D chemistry tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors evaluate on a curated twelve-task dataset with task-specific metrics and baselines, reporting performance beyond specialized state-of-the-art models for crystal structure prediction and property-conditional molecule generation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify computational cost or generalization beyond the curated tasks, leaving deployment efficiency and broader transfer uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Nahual: A Sequence Model for Language and Atoms

title: A Density Functional Tight Binding Model for Rapid Screening of Spin-Orbit-Coupling-Driven Topological Properties in Bismuth
authors: Nir Goldman, Ben Hourahine
abstract: We present a transferable Density Functional Tight Binding (DFTB) model for bismuth with explicit spin-orbit coupling that enables exploration of the structural degrees of freedom governing topological properties with minimal computational resources. We have used our DFTB model to run high-throughput calculations at a scale that would be significantly more expensive with standard Kohn-Sham Density Functional Theory (DFT) to determine a strain-buckling map of electronic and topological properties for bismuthene, where we identify regions of band gap closure and band inversion as a function of structural parameters. We show that our approach yields an accurate band structure for the rhombohedral phase, where small band gaps exist at or near time-reversal-invariant momentum (TRIM) points. We then demonstrate the transferability of our model to bismuth properties not included in our training data through determination of the rhombohedral phase phonon density of states and energetic ordering of additional bismuth solid phases. Finally, we have validated our topological predictions through comparison to DFT results for the optimized bilayer geometries, a band inversion order parameter, and the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ invariant as a function of monolayer unit cell length. Our efforts establish DFTB as a rigorous approach for topological characterization while yielding approximately three orders of magnitude increase in computational efficiency relative to DFT. Our model can thus serve as a computational tool for topological materials discovery by enabling large-scale computational screening to address the potentially complex relationship between physical-chemical properties and the resulting topological classification.

infographic.key_insight: A bismuth density functional tight binding model with explicit spin–orbit coupling maps topology-related electronic changes at approximately 1,000 times the computational efficiency of DFT.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model enables large-scale screening of how strain and buckling affect bismuthene’s electronic structure and topological classification.
method: Develop a transferable bismuth DFTB model with explicit spin–orbit coupling.
Screen bismuthene structures to map band gap closure and band inversion versus strain and buckling.
Validate electronic, structural, vibrational, and topological predictions against DFT.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate rhombohedral band structures, transferability tests on phonons and additional solid phases, and DFT comparisons of optimized bilayers, band inversion, and the Z₂ invariant.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is specific to the tested bismuth structures; accuracy for other materials or unexplored structural regimes remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: A Density Functional Tight Binding Model for Rapid Screening of Spin-Orbit-Coupling-Driven Topological Properties in Bismuth

title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
authors: Yury Lysogorskiy, Anton Bochkarev, Ralf Drautz
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.

infographic.key_insight: ACE and its graph generalization GRACE provide a common basis for comparing interatomic potentials, revealing that much architectural diversity comes from nonlinear parameterization, layer coupling and optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Choosing MLIPs along an accuracy–speed Pareto front can reduce atomistic simulation costs while preserving the accuracy needed for materials discovery.
method: Represent classical potentials and modern MLIPs in a canonical expansion of single-particle functions.
Analyze linear scaling with system size and, at fixed tensor-decomposition rank, model complexity.
Compare accuracy and computational cost across model depths and basis truncations.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Matbench Discovery, three- to five-layer models approach deeper-model accuracy, while Pareto-front truncations of one basis span more than two orders of magnitude in cost.
infographic.watch_item: Training data ultimately determine MLIP quality, so efficient architecture alone does not ensure reliable predictions.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials

title: Swift Heavy Ion Tracks in Polymorphs of Titanium Dioxide: The Effects of Electron Beam and Crystal Structures
authors: Xiaoting Jia, Lijun Xu, Ruslan A. Rymzhanov, Wenqiang Liu, Peipei Hu, Shengxia Zhang
abstract: Swift heavy ion (SHI) irradiation generates nanoscale damage in materials, offering opportunities for controlled modification of structural properties. Understanding the fundamental processes governing damage formation in altered regions remains a longstanding challenge. This work explores how crystal structure influences swift heavy ion-induced damage formation and evolution in rutile and anatase TiO2. Combining transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate how differences in atomic arrangement govern track morphology and structural recovery. Although irradiation produces amorphous tracks in both polymorphs, their morphologies differ considerably. In rutile, tracks develop pronounced diameter variations, forming hourglass-like structures, whereas in anatase they retain a relatively uniform cylindrical shape. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that these differences arise from the distinct recrystallization behavior of the two crystal structures during rapid cooling, leading to different pathways of track evolution and recovery. Particular attention is paid to electron beam induced effects during TEM characterization, which can substantially modify the structure and apparent morphology of ion tracks. Prolonged electron beam exposure promotes the recrystallization of initially amorphous tracks and surface hillocks, accompanied by the development of Fresnel contrast. These findings highlight the importance of understanding beam-induced transformations for the reliable interpretation of TEM observations of radiation-damaged materials.

infographic.key_insight: Crystal-structure-dependent recrystallization produces hourglass-like ion tracks in rutile TiO2 but relatively uniform cylindrical tracks in anatase.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding track recovery can guide irradiation-based modification of TiO2 and improve interpretation of radiation-damage microscopy.
method: Compare swift heavy ion damage in rutile and anatase TiO2.
Use TEM to characterize track morphology and electron-beam-induced changes.
Use molecular dynamics to examine recrystallization during rapid cooling.
infographic.evidence_signal: TEM observations show distinct track morphologies in the two polymorphs, while simulations attribute these differences to their recrystallization behavior.
infographic.watch_item: Prolonged TEM electron-beam exposure can recrystallize amorphous tracks and surface hillocks, altering the apparent damage morphology.
infographic.paper_title: Swift Heavy Ion Tracks in Polymorphs of Titanium Dioxide: The Effects of Electron Beam and Crystal Structures

title: What Do LLMs Use to Judge Synthesis Recipes? An Experimental Analysis on 240 Solid-State Syntheses
authors: Derek van Tilborg, Laura-Bianca Pasca, Harry Sevi, Kyle Reeves, Thomas Loux, Aikaterini Flessa Savvidou
abstract: Inorganic materials discovery is increasingly limited by synthesis rather than by material design. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted to propose synthesis conditions with little experimental evidence of their capabilities and biases. Here, we carry out an experimental synthesis benchmark of 240 experiments across eight known and unknown inorganic oxides and subsequently evaluate an LLM as a zero-shot ranker over fixed banks of solid-state synthesis recipes. For each pair of recipes for the same oxide target, `GPT-5.6-Sol` selects the recipe expected to yield higher target-phase purity. We aggregate these pairwise preferences using a regularized Bradley-Terry model to obtain a ranked list of synthesis recipes for a given target material. By comparison with the actual purity, obtained through X-ray diffraction, we measure `GPT-5.6-Sol`'s performance as a zero-shot ranker (0.72 pairwise accuracy). By selective removal of the information exposed to the model during this ranking, we conclude that ranking is driven predominantly by thermal features, with reaction chemistry modulating the effect. Ranking accuracy tracks the purity-temperature correlation by target (Spearman ρ= 0.91\), \(p = 0.002\), and on the six thermally-driven targets withholding all chemical identity hardly impacts performance (0.68) compared to withholding temperature (0.56). Ranking performance was higher on known than unknown targets, but the group-level difference was not statistically conclusive. The methodological choices highlight the need for more experimentally validated synthesis benchmarks and position LLMs as a thermally informed prior.

infographic.key_insight: LLM judgments of solid-state synthesis recipes were driven mainly by thermal features, with reaction chemistry modulating their effect.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLMs may provide a thermally informed prior for prioritizing synthesis recipes, but their rankings still require experimental validation.
method: Benchmark 240 synthesis experiments across eight known and unknown inorganic oxides.
Use GPT-5.6-Sol to compare recipe pairs, then aggregate preferences with a regularized Bradley–Terry model.
Evaluate rankings against X-ray diffraction purity measurements and selectively withhold recipe information.
infographic.evidence_signal: Pairwise accuracy was 0.72 overall; on six thermally driven targets, accuracy was 0.68 without chemical identity versus 0.56 without temperature.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover fixed recipe banks for only eight oxides and do not establish reliable generation of new synthesis recipes.
infographic.paper_title: What Do LLMs Use to Judge Synthesis Recipes? An Experimental Analysis on 240 Solid-State Syntheses

title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
authors: Gengyue Dong, Ye Wei, Zheng Zhu, Yidong Han, Jiale Miao, Xiaojun Jia
abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

infographic.key_insight: SkillBuffBench is designed to isolate how file-based Agent Skills and memory affect research-task performance across agent harnesses and models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark could help engineers assess whether curated or automatically selected Skills improve scientific workflows enough to justify their cost and runtime.
method: Compare no Skill, a curated Skill and automatic invocation from an installed library.
Cross Skill access with memory off/on, four harnesses and multiple proprietary and open-weight models.
Use expert-contributed materials science and biology tasks, deterministic verifiers and paired task-level bootstrap uncertainty.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation is in progress; the protocol reports task scores alongside cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time, but no performance results are available yet.
infographic.watch_item: Skill benefits remain unproven, and generalization will depend on task coverage and the installed Skill library.
infographic.paper_title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory

title: Dynamics and transport in LiF using classical and machine learned interatomic potentials
authors: Harvey L. Devereux, Margaret-Ann Withington, Alin M. Elena, Cillian Cockrell, Kostya Trachenko
abstract: We perform molecular dynamics simulations of molten Lithium Fluoride, comparing the classical Buckingham and Born-Huggins-Mayer potentials with machine-learnt interatomic potentials - the MACE-MP-0b3 (small) foundation model potential, and a fine-tuned version thereof. We find that the MACE-MP-0b3, out-of-the-box, is able to accurately reproduce the experimental shear viscosity across the liquid state comparable with polarisable potentials despite not itself being polarisable. Previous viscosities computed using classical potentials are under-predicted, which has previously been attributed to a suppressed melting temperature. Prompted by this we compare the melting points of these potentials. We find that the machine-learnt potentials address the significant underestimation of the melting point of the classical potentials, though the refined potential and the foundation model differ significantly between themselves. We probe the microscopic structure and dynamics of each model to further elucidate the considerable change in viscosity between classical and machine-learnt potentials. We find that, despite their lower melting temperature, classical potentials produce considerably stiffer, higher frequency, single-particle and collective charge-transport dynamics on account of their fixed charges. However, in the long-wavelength limit, the many-body machine-learnt potentials feature more elastic collective motion that governs the diffusion of momentum and is therefore responsible for the enhanced shear viscosity.

infographic.key_insight: For molten LiF, machine-learned potentials improve melting-point predictions over classical models, while the out-of-the-box MACE foundation model accurately reproduces experimental shear viscosity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Machine-learned potentials could improve molten-salt transport modeling by capturing collective momentum dynamics that classical fixed-charge models miss.
method: Run molecular dynamics with Buckingham and Born–Huggins–Mayer classical potentials.
Compare MACE-MP-0b3 (small) with a fine-tuned version.
Evaluate melting points, shear viscosity, microscopic structure, and transport dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports experimental viscosity agreement for the foundation model comparable to polarizable potentials, with enhanced viscosity linked to more elastic long-wavelength collective motion.
infographic.watch_item: The foundation and fine-tuned models predict substantially different melting points, so fine-tuning should not be assumed to improve every property.
infographic.paper_title: Dynamics and transport in LiF using classical and machine learned interatomic potentials

title: Energetics of Coherent Heterophase Interfaces: Separating Chemical and Strain Contributions
authors: Adolfo Salgado-Casanova, Jacob Pietryga, Yi Xia, Chris Wolverton
abstract: Coherent interfacial energies govern the formation and evolution of multiphase microstructures, but their calculation is complicated by the elastic energy required to accommodate lattice mismatch. Here, we construct a high-throughput DFT database of 365 coherent FCC/FCC, BCC/BCC, and HCP/HCP interfaces involving 41 metallic elements and lattice mismatches of up to 25%. We use the supercell approach, consisting of constructing superlattices of different thicknesses to separate the coherency strain energy from the chemical contribution to the interfacial energy. We classify the results according to the long-range ordering tendency of each binary system and the sign of the calculated interfacial energy. Most phase-separating systems exhibit positive interfacial energies, whereas most compound-ordering systems exhibit negative values, reflecting favorable unlike-atom bonding. Exceptions show that the chemical preference at a particular interface need not coincide with bulk phase behavior: coherency strain can oppose ordering, and stable compounds can adopt structures distinct from the calculated superlattices. No clear correlation of interfacial energy with lattice mismatch is observed, whereas coherency strain energy increases with mismatch. For phase-separating systems, the lowest interfacial energies generally occur along the closest-packed orientations, while this trend is absent for ordering systems. Comparisons with reported interfacial energies and binary phase diagrams show qualitative consistency, although quantitative agreement varies with reference states, structural constraints, and temperature. The database provides a systematic reference for metallic coherent heterophase interfaces and demonstrates the importance of separating strain and chemical energy contributions when interpreting alloy behavior.

infographic.key_insight: Separating chemical interface energy from coherency strain reveals that lattice mismatch raises strain energy but does not clearly predict interfacial energy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The database can inform alloy microstructure modeling by distinguishing interfacial bonding preferences from the elastic cost of maintaining coherency.
method: Construct coherent FCC/FCC, BCC/BCC, and HCP/HCP superlattices for high-throughput DFT calculations.
Vary superlattice thickness to separate coherency strain energy from chemical interfacial energy.
Classify interfaces by energy sign and bulk ordering tendency.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 365 interfaces involving 41 metallic elements and lattice mismatches up to 25%, most phase-separating systems show positive interfacial energies, while most compound-ordering systems show negative values.
infographic.watch_item: Quantitative comparisons depend on reference states, structural constraints, and temperature; interface bonding preferences need not match bulk phase behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Energetics of Coherent Heterophase Interfaces: Separating Chemical and Strain Contributions

title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows
authors: Yuchen Zhang, Taolin Han, Jinghang Wang, Jinxin Wang, Yun Wu, Wai Yuet Chiu
abstract: Language models are increasingly being used as agents capable of planning and executing projects, as well as refining their actions through feedback. This shift raises a question: can current agents complete projects like real scientists? To examine this question, we introduce SciWorkBench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' abilities on real science tasks across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics. SciWorkBench is built from peer-reviewed literature or expert-contributed research scenarios. We also propose a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts, which can categorize most tasks in SciWorkBench. Each task covers one or more stages of this framework. We evaluate up-to-date models within the Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks under a unified execution and grading protocol. The best-performing agent achieves a mean score of 57.38, indicating that current agents still struggle with realistic scientific workflows. Our failure analysis identifies three recurring weaknesses at the workflow level: difficulty translating scientific knowledge into task-specific procedures, weak integration of evidence across different modalities, and limited capacity for scientific self-correction. These findings highlight the importance of workflow-based evaluation for measuring progress toward reliable AI systems for scientific research.

infographic.key_insight: SciWorkBench evaluates AI agents on realistic scientific workflows, revealing persistent gaps in executing research projects reliably.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For materials research teams, the benchmark highlights the need to validate agents across complete workflows rather than isolated scientific tasks.
method: Build tasks from peer-reviewed literature and expert-contributed scenarios across four scientific domains.
Categorize tasks using a unified scientific analysis framework validated by domain experts.
Evaluate models in Claude Code and Codex agent frameworks with unified execution and grading.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across biology, chemistry, materials science, and physics tasks, the best-performing agent achieved a mean score of 57.38.
infographic.watch_item: Agents struggle with task-specific procedures, multimodal evidence integration, and scientific self-correction; the abstract does not report materials-specific performance.
infographic.paper_title: SciWorkBench: A Benchmark for Real Scientific Workflows

title: Magnetic History and Field Sweep Rate Effects on Transformation Hysteresis in $\mathrm{Ni}_{41}\mathrm{Co}_{9}\mathrm{Mn}_{31.5}\mathrm{Ga}_{18.5}$
authors: T. Kihara, T. Miyakawa, D. Imatomi, X. Xu, Y. Ishii, H. Hayashi
abstract: Hysteresis in magnetic-field-induced structural phase transformations is a major obstacle to the application of metamagnetic shape memory alloys. One promising approach to reduce hysteresis is to utilize a metastable martensitic state generated by magnetic-field cycling. However, the mechanism by which the metastable state reduces hysteresis remains unclear. Here, microsecond pulsed-field magnetization measurements are used to investigate the transformation kinetics of $\mathrm{Ni}_{41}\mathrm{Co}_{9}\mathrm{Mn}_{31.5}\mathrm{Ga}_{18.5}$. Magnetic-field cycling reduces the hysteresis width by approximately 50-60%, demonstrating that substantial suppression persists on a microsecond timescale. Comparison with millisecond pulsed-field measurements suggests that the reverse martensitic transformation field is more sensitive to the field sweep rate for the metastable martensite than for the initial martensite. Possible explanations include enhanced thermal activation associated with a lower effective activation barrier and differences in the athermal contribution arising from different metastable martensitic microstructures.

infographic.key_insight: Magnetic-field cycling reduces transformation hysteresis in Ni₄₁Co₉Mn₃₁.₅Ga₁₈.₅ by approximately 50–60%, with suppression persisting on a microsecond timescale.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Magnetic-history control could reduce hysteresis losses in fast-switching metamagnetic shape memory devices, but field sweep rate must be considered.
method: Use microsecond pulsed-field magnetization to probe transformation kinetics.
Compare initial and field-cycled metastable martensitic states.
Compare microsecond results with millisecond pulsed-field measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: The measurements show approximately 50–60% hysteresis narrowing after cycling and suggest greater sweep-rate sensitivity of the reverse transformation field in metastable martensite.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism remains unresolved: lower effective activation barriers and microstructure-dependent athermal contributions are proposed explanations, not established causes.
infographic.paper_title: Magnetic History and Field Sweep Rate Effects on Transformation Hysteresis in $\mathrm{Ni}_{41}\mathrm{Co}_{9}\mathrm{Mn}_{31.5}\mathrm{Ga}_{18.5}$

title: AlCoCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Nanoparticle Melting and Solidification: A Classical Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study
authors: O. I. Kushnerov
abstract: The processes of melting and solidification of an AlCoCuFeNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticle with a diameter of about 10 nm were studied by classical molecular dynamics simulation using an embedded atom model potential. Three cooling rates, 10^11, 10^12, and 10^13 K/s, were considered. Melting and crystallization behavior were characterized through the temperature dependence of the potential energy. Structural evolution was analyzed using adaptive common-neighbor analysis (CNA) and radial distribution functions (RDF). The results show that the final structure changes from amorphous to crystalline as the cooling rate decreases. A pronounced temperature hysteresis associated with melting and crystallization was also observed.

infographic.key_insight: Slower cooling shifts an approximately 10 nm AlCoCuFeNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticle from an amorphous toward a crystalline final structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Cooling-rate control may help tune atomic order in high-entropy alloy nanoparticles during thermal processing.
method: Classical molecular dynamics with an embedded atom model potential.
Cooling rates of 10^11, 10^12, and 10^13 K/s.
Potential-energy tracking, adaptive common-neighbor analysis, and radial distribution functions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations showed cooling-rate-dependent final structures and pronounced temperature hysteresis between melting and crystallization.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern an approximately 10 nm simulated particle at extremely rapid cooling rates; transfer to experiments or larger particles requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: AlCoCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Nanoparticle Melting and Solidification: A Classical Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study

title: Combined magnetic and structural transition state in first-principles calculations
authors: Samare Rostami, Xavier Gonze
abstract: We present a generalized nudged elastic band (NEB) implementation within potential-based constrained density-functional theory (cDFT) for calculating transition pathways that simultaneously optimize atomic, lattice, and magnetic degrees of freedom. Unlike standard fixed-cell NEB calculations restricted to atomic displacements, our framework consistently couples atomic forces, stresses, and spin torques. The method supports fixed- and variable-cell approaches for collinear and non- collinear magnetic configurations, by incorporating magnetic torques and generalized cell coordinates within the NEB optimization. To validate the methodology, we present benchmark calculations for representative magnetostructural systems. Specifically, we investigate the bcc-to-hcp transformation in Fe and the antiferromagnetic-to-ferromagnetic transition in FeRh using the variable-cell formalism. Furthermore, we examine spin-reversal processes in two-dimensional CrI3 to analyze the influence of spin-orbit coupling on transition paths and their associated energy barriers.

infographic.key_insight: A generalized nudged elastic band framework finds transition pathways by jointly optimizing atomic positions, lattice geometry, and magnetic configurations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method enables coupled magnetostructural barrier calculations relevant to designing magnetic materials and devices.
method: Integrates NEB with potential-based constrained density-functional theory.
Couples atomic forces, cell stresses, and magnetic spin torques.
Supports fixed or variable cells and collinear or non-collinear magnetism.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks examine bcc-to-hcp Fe, antiferromagnetic-to-ferromagnetic FeRh, and spin reversal in two-dimensional CrI3 with attention to spin-orbit coupling.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative accuracy or computational-cost results, limiting assessment of scalability.
infographic.paper_title: Combined magnetic and structural transition state in first-principles calculations

title: Large-scale Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials in LAMMPS
authors: Lorenzo Piersante, Anirudh Raju Natarajan
abstract: Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics (MCMD) simulations are widely used to study the properties of materials at the mesoscale. Simulations with hundreds of thousands of atoms usually rely on empirical potentials because MCMD with machine-learning interatomic potentials is impractical at this scale in existing implementations. Here, we introduce a hybrid MPI/OpenMP scheme for MCMD with Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) potentials in LAMMPS. Monte Carlo moves are evaluated from local energy changes and carried out in parallel over MPI ranks, while molecular dynamics is parallelized over OpenMP threads. At a fixed number of CPUs, the wall time of the Monte Carlo moves decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks. Larger simulation cells also reduce the statistical errors of free energy calculations because thermal fluctuations decrease with system size. We demonstrate the scheme by calculating free energies of the HCP and BCC phases in the strongly anharmonic Hf--Ti system and by simulating zirconium segregation in a nanocrystalline copper sample of 670,000 atoms. For Cu--Zr, an ACE potential and an empirical potential predict similar grain boundary compositions but different amounts of zirconium dissolved in the grains. The scheme makes MCMD simulations with machine-learning interatomic potentials practical at the length scales of microstructure.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid MPI/OpenMP implementation in LAMMPS makes Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials practical for microstructure-scale simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables machine-learning-potential studies of phase stability and grain-boundary segregation in systems containing hundreds of thousands of atoms.
method: Evaluate Monte Carlo moves using local energy changes.
Parallelize Monte Carlo moves across MPI ranks and molecular dynamics over OpenMP threads.
Use larger simulation cells to reduce thermal fluctuations and free-energy statistical errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Demonstrations include HCP/BCC free energies in Hf–Ti and zirconium segregation in 670,000-atom nanocrystalline copper; at fixed CPU count, Monte Carlo wall time decreases by a factor equal to the number of MPI ranks.
infographic.watch_item: Potential choice remains consequential: ACE and empirical potentials predict similar grain-boundary compositions but different zirconium solubility within copper grains.
infographic.paper_title: Large-scale Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations with Atomic Cluster Expansion potentials in LAMMPS

title: Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy
authors: Miguel Tenorio, James Chapman
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) show promise for predicting materials properties, but interpretability remains a challenge, particularly understanding whether attributed feature importance reflects physical reality or statistical artifacts. Here, we present a methods validation study that deliberately overfits a physics-aware GNN ensemble to probe the robustness of feature-ranking approaches. Using the CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy system with three stoichiometries, we train GNNs to predict decomposition enthalpies from DFT-calculated structures while explicitly constraining output weights to encode feature importance. By design, our dataset is limited (approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways) to control compositional complexity and enable precise interrogation of local chemistry effects. We validate that feature rankings capture meaningful local-environment information through a series of atomic swap perturbations: perturbing individual atomic sites and re-ranking features reveals spatial decay consistent with the GNN's interaction cutoff, confirming that weights encode neighbor-shell effects rather than global stoichiometric artifacts alone. Results demonstrate that feature attribution methods can remain physically interpretable even under overfitting, provided validation is rigorous. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy interpretability in materials GNNs and sets the stage for scaling to multiple chemistries and testing generalization across compositional spaces.

infographic.key_insight: Local atomic-swap tests indicate that GNN feature rankings can reflect physically meaningful neighbor-shell effects even in deliberately overfit models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Perturbation-based validation can help engineers assess whether materials-model explanations capture local chemistry rather than global composition artifacts.
method: Train a deliberately overfit, physics-aware GNN ensemble on DFT-derived CoMoFeNiCu decomposition enthalpies.
Constrain output weights to encode feature importance.
Swap individual atomic sites and re-rank features to test spatial sensitivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three stoichiometries and approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways, attribution changes showed spatial decay consistent with the GNN interaction cutoff.
infographic.watch_item: Interpretability validation in this limited, deliberately overfit setting does not establish predictive generalization to new compositions or chemistries.
infographic.paper_title: Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy
